title: Guess the page, not the middle
hook: Can aiming by value beat halving? It depends on how the values are spread.

knows: binary search opens the middle of a sorted list (binary-search)
doesNotKnow: that you can aim at a position from the value you want
that aiming by value backfires on unevenly spread data

misconception: Opening the middle is always the fastest way to search a sorted list.
objective: The learner can explain that interpolation search guesses a position from the value, finds an evenly spread value in one look, and can need many more looks than halving when the values are bunched (cubes).

claims.text: On 100 sorted values 10, 20, ..., 1000, guessing the position of 730 from its value finds it in 1 look, at position 73 (the 73rd value, counting from 1).
claims.source: Builder's node run: guess = lo + floor((x - a[lo]) * (hi - lo) / (a[hi] - a[lo])) gives 0-based index 72 = position 73, and a[72] = 730 = 10 x 73. Every value on the even list takes 1 look (node, all 100 targets). The brief's 'position 72' is the 0-based index; the stage counts positions 1-100.

claims.text: Halving (opening the position floor((lo + hi) / 2) each time) needs 6 looks for 730 on the even list, 7 looks for 729,000, 6 for 1,000 and 5 for 9,261 on the cube list, and never more than 7 for any value.
claims.source: Builder's node run of binary search with 0-based mid = floor((lo + hi) / 2), counting each opened position: 730 -> 6; cubes 729,000 -> 7, 1,000 -> 6, 9,261 -> 5; maximum over all 100 values on either list = 7. The halving count depends on the floor-midpoint convention. The wireframe's '(halving 7)' beside 9,261 is the maximum, not that value's count; the stage computes the real count.

claims.text: On the cubes 1, 8, 27, ..., 1,000,000 the same aiming rule needs 4 looks for 729,000, 10 for 1,000 and 21 for 9,261; 21 is the most for any of the 100 values.
claims.source: Builder's node run of the same rule on the cubes list: 729,000 -> 4 (positions 73, 88, 89, 90); 1,000 -> 10 (positions 1..10); 9,261 -> 21 (positions 1..21); maximum 21 at 9,261; mean 8.86 looks against 5.8 for halving. 8,000 takes 20.

claims.text: Aiming by value is like opening a dictionary near the back for 'W': it works well when values are spread evenly and can be worse than halving when they are not.
claims.source: Analogy; the two lists on the stage are the evidence (1 look against 6 on even values; 21 against 5 on cubes for 9,261; but 4 against 7 on cubes for 729,000, so aiming is not always worse).

claims.text: On the cubes the aim line falls short at each look because the straight line from the low end to the high end sits well below the bending dots, so each look moves one position.
claims.source: Node trace for 9,261 shows probes 1, 2, ..., 21 in order: each aim lands one position past the last. Shown on the stage as the ticks crawling from the left edge.

recall.question: A sorted list holds 100 values, but nearly all are tiny and a few are huge. You guess each position from the value you want. Compared with halving, aiming by value is likely to be...
options: slower, because the straight-line guess keeps falling short
still one look, because the list is sorted
faster, because it uses more information
recall.why: Aiming assumes the values are spread evenly. When they are bunched, as with cubes, each guess lands near the start and the search crawls.
